summary:
Tarpuy is a web tool aimed at farming families in Peru and the agronomists who support them. Its purpose is to bridge the lack of technical assistance in the field and translate complex agroclimatic data into clear recommendations to address climate change.

Through a five-step process, the platform integrates local satellite information from NASA and NOAA, frost alerts, El Niño and La Niña warnings, soil and irrigation estimates, and market prices. Using this data, it proposes crop rotations for forty-eight crops across twelve zones in the coast, highlands, and jungle.

As a result, it delivers estimated gross income per hectare and a downloadable planting and harvesting calendar. The application features a simple mode for farmers and a technical mode for specialists, operates without costs or complex registrations, and provides guiding alerts that help protect an entire agricultural season's work.
details:
Tarpuy —Quechua for “sowing”— is a free, bilingual web app that helps Peruvian family farmers decide what to plant and in what order. In five steps the farmer marks the plot, reads the local climate in plain words, sees which crops fit that zone and month with their water needs and estimated gross income, describes soil and irrigation, and chooses up to two priorities. The app then returns a three-to-six campaign rotation with short reasons, a water–soil–climate–money traffic light, El Niño and frost alerts, a downloadable calendar and a WhatsApp summary. A simple mode keeps the decision and the action at the front, while a technical mode preserves every number, source and transparency panel.

The benefits are practical. Tarpuy reduces campaign risk by comparing available water with what each crop really needs instead of averaging the problem away; it favors rotations that cover the soil, fix nitrogen and limit erosion; and it frames income as a gross reference per hectare and year, explicitly before costs, so options can be compared without promising a sale price. Because it works offline, the last plan and the field-report form keep working with poor signal, and its language avoids jargon, so a farmer without technical assistance can use it alone.

The intended impact is that a family without technical assistance ends with a better-founded decision rather than more data. In the short term we aim to validate the app with three to five farmers and technicians through a five-task field guide, with success defined as at least four of the five tasks completed without help. In the medium term, the expectation is adoption of rotations that preserve soil and water and fewer campaigns lost to drought, frost or excess rain. In the longer term, a moderated base of farmer experiences, shown only after five approved reports, should feed recommendations back to the next family in the same zone. Tarpuy is a working, technically verified prototype; field validation and agronomic review are still pending and are documented as such.

We built Tarpuy with vanilla JavaScript ES modules, HTML and hand-written CSS on the client, with no bundler and no runtime npm dependencies, and a Node.js 18+ server that uses only the native HTTP module. Data come from open sources: ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo for local climate, NASA POWER for trends and as a fallback, the NOAA CPC Oceanic Niño Index for El Niño and La Niña alerts, ISRIC SoilGrids for soil properties, and Microsoft Planetary Computer for elevation, land cover, Sentinel-2 NDVI and MODIS vegetation indices. The map uses Leaflet served locally, with NASA GIBS, Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap as fallbacks. On the device we rely on a service worker for offline behaviour, IndexedDB for the plan and the report queue, Canvas to re-encode photos before sharing, speech synthesis for the “Listen” button and WhatsApp links for sharing. No special hardware is required: development happens on a Windows PC and the app runs in ordinary Android and iPhone browsers. Quality is enforced with the built-in Node test runner (73 tests), a custom linter, browser audits written against the Chrome DevTools Protocol and 80 reproducible screenshots.

Creativity shows in the product decisions as much as in the visuals. The main screen does not present a form but a decision, followed by three short reasons and a traffic light, while sources and numbers remain available in the detail panels. The simple mode is not a watered-down version but the same recommendation explained without jargon —a glossary and an automated audit fail the build if technical terms reappear— so a farmer and a technician can discuss exactly the same plan. We treated honesty as a design feature: when NASA POWER returned missing soil-moisture values we stopped calling it a measurement and labelled it as a model, and when a dataset required a login we documented it and left it out instead of faking it. Privacy is built into the flow: the field report asks for one of twelve reference zones, never the exact location, and photos are re-encoded before they leave the phone. Among the factors we considered were intermittent connectivity, low digital literacy, small screens, accessibility with 44-pixel touch targets and 14-pixel secondary text, the risk of agricultural misinformation, which is why comments mentioning doses or agrochemicals are flagged for review, and a deliberate geographic scope: Tarpuy covers Peru only, and version 0.14.0 adds a contract that classifies queries as Peruvian, foreign, ambiguous or cross-border and rejects coordinates outside the country.
